name: Yara Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you tell me is confidential. What is an ordinary workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Yara Hansen, 43, and I repair doors, stairs and partitions in occupied flats for a subcontractor. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of site experience, so I can handle an ordinary repair, though I still ask for help on an unfamiliar wall. The pay is low for this work because we get three or four days in some weeks. I have never used an AI tool; a clear job sheet and enough paid hours would help more.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household need from those hours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner cleans a school on term-time hours, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have less than a month of expenses saved and only a few similar employers nearby. A cancelled Friday can turn the grocery card into next month’s problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a faster office form will not put plaster back on a wall or hang a flat door. I have never used an AI tool, and I would rather get a clear job sheet from the supervisor. I'd also say that a quiet technology story does not fix short weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've done repairs for years and have a trade certificate, but this subcontractor gives me only three or four days some weeks. My partner cleans a school on term-time hours. We have less than a month's bills saved against the mortgage, and there are only a few other crews nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid flat-repair shift and ask the supervisor on Thursday for the next week's roster. In the first year I'd go to the union branch meeting about minimum notice for cancelled days. We would keep the old washing machine running rather than buy a new one, unless it finally breaks beyond repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even with AI doing little. The mortgage letter arrives whether I have had three days or five. I do not need a robot to make a thin week hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on a short week recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat was not ready for repairs, so I lost Friday’s pay after buying materials for the week. The supervisor found a day at another building, but only after I called twice. We paid the mortgage and put groceries on the card until my partner’s school cleaning pay came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union branch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Several of us had shifts cancelled the night before. I want the branch to ask for a paid notice period, so a worker can plan bills and childcare. I do not expect one meeting to create more building jobs in this area.

say: I would say a faster **office form** does not repair a flat.
I would say small AI changes cannot fix **short weeks**.
think: I have a **trade certificate** and experience, yet receive only three or four days some weeks.
Our **under-one-month cushion** and few local crews leave the mortgage exposed.
do: Keep every paid **flat-repair shift** and ask for the roster each Thursday.
Attend the **union branch** meeting about notice for cancelled days.
Keep the **old washing machine** instead of replacing it while hours are uncertain.
feel: **Anxious** about the mortgage even when AI changes little.
S0.quote: I do not need a robot to make a thin week hard.
fieldNote: Yara’s baseline worry comes from **cancelled Fridays** and less than a month saved, not speculation about AI.
Her trade certificate has not overcome **local scarcity** or short subcontractor weeks.

steps.text: Keep paid flat-repair shifts and ask for next week’s roster every Thursday
Attend the union branch meeting on paid notice for cancelled days
Keep the working washing machine rather than buying a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the repair crew the office may book jobs and order doors faster, but a bad wall still needs a worker who can read it. I would ask whether the new schedule guarantees days or just packs more jobs into fewer visits. Our union should see the numbers before the contractor calls it progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork part of my work is small, but I can imagine the contractor joining visits and sending one crew instead of two. One lost day a fortnight would hurt us now. My partner’s school cleaning hours could also be rearranged by a smarter schedule, so neither wage feels completely safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd write down every cancelled day and the reason the supervisor gives. I'd bring the log to the union representative and ask the contractor for a minimum weekly roster. In the first year I'd keep applying for the few local repair openings as they appear, while continuing paid shifts here; I would not leave for a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More anxious. Faster booking could help a tenant get a safe door sooner, which matters. I still need to know whether the worker who hangs it gets a full week's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many cancelled days would force a change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two in a month would put us back on the grocery card, and the card is already carrying last month’s short week. I would ask my sister to collect the children if I got an extra day at short notice. I do not want her doing that forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you apply locally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two housing repair firms and a small school maintenance crew. I know people at one firm, but they are not always hiring. I would send a real application when a paid place opens, not keep a list of names and call it a plan.

say: I would ask whether **faster bookings** mean full weeks or fewer paid visits.
I would bring the **union** real roster numbers before accepting a good-news story.
think: Losing **one day a fortnight** would hurt our mortgage budget now.
My partner’s **cleaning hours** could also change with smarter scheduling.
do: Log every **cancelled day** and take the record to the union representative.
Ask the contractor for a **minimum weekly roster**.
Apply for **local repair openings** when paid vacancies appear.
feel: More **anxious** about hours, despite possible faster repairs for tenants.
S1.quote: I would send a real application when a paid place opens, not keep a list of names and call it a plan.
fieldNote: Her **day-by-day log** turns a vague concern into evidence for union bargaining over paid hours.
Only **three nearby employers** are plausible alternatives, and current credit-card groceries show little room for another lost day.

steps.text: Keep paid flat-repair shifts while recording cancelled days
Take the cancelled-day log to the union representative and request a minimum roster
Apply to local repair firms when paid vacancies appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office and planning change by 2028, then robots able to do our hands-on repairs arrive around 2031. Our crew cannot wait for the first machine before asking about jobs. I would want the contractor and union in the same room with a written plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots can do the repair work. My partner’s school cleaning is hands-on too, so the 2031 date could reach both of us. With less than a month's expenses saved and few builders nearby, I expect a big wage loss if this subcontractor buys robots. That possibility has already kept me awake at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking every paid shift and ask the union representative to demand a written staffing and paid training plan this month. I'd apply to the school maintenance crew now if it advertises a paid vacancy, though robots could later do that work too. In the first year after 2028 we'd cut the small holiday fund and ask my sister whether she could cover school pickup if I found work farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make applications, but a month without my wage would put the mortgage in danger. I resent being told to wait calmly when the first hit could be the office and the next could be both our hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would come first if pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage and power would come ahead of the children’s sports fees. We would speak to the lender before missing a payment, not hide the letter. I would ask my sister for pickup help so I could take a job farther away, not ask her to pay our loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is school maintenance a safe route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a capable robot could repair school doors as well as flats. It is a paid opening I can apply for now, with a known supervisor, while I still have some time. I cannot invent a protected trade on the spot.

say: I would tell coworkers **2028 planning AI** comes before 2031 repair robots.
I would ask the contractor and union for a **written staffing plan**.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach both repair work and possibly school cleaning.
Less than a month saved and few local jobs make **major wage loss** likely enough to keep me awake.
do: Keep every paid **repair shift** and press the union for staffing terms.
Apply for a paid **school maintenance vacancy** if advertised.
Cut the **holiday fund** and ask my sister about pickup if distant work opens.
feel: **Alarmed** by a likely major income gap and the immediate mortgage risk.
S2.quote: I cannot invent a protected trade on the spot.
fieldNote: Yara expects **two hands-on wages** to face capable robots around 2031, on top of current short weeks.
Her proposed school-maintenance move is **paid work now**, with explicit acknowledgement that robots could take it later.

steps.text: Keep every paid flat-repair shift while the contractor offers work
Ask the union to demand a written staffing and paid training plan
Apply for a paid school maintenance opening if advertised
Cancel contributions to the small holiday fund after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and robots reach site repairs about 2034. Five years is time for employers to explain what work remains, if they are honest. I would still demand notice of cancelled days now, because the family cannot live on a future promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 the desk side changes and at 51 the robots can do my repairs. The children will be older, but the mortgage will still need paying unless our wages improve. I could prepare more with five years, yet I cannot build a savings cushion out of three-day weeks by wishing it so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the repair job and ask the union to bargain for paid hours to learn any new site equipment once it is proven safe. If the contractor offers funded hands-on instruction during paid shifts, I'd enrol; I would not pay for a course with our grocery money. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for the school maintenance crew if it still has openings and keep the union roster log going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the longer date lets me breathe between bills. I can ask for paid training before robots arrive. The biggest pressure is still the current roster, not a machine I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make new equipment safe enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supervisor who has used it should show the stop control and watch me on a real repair. I am slow to trust new gear, and I will not learn beside tenants with no safety check. Paid practice would let me learn without cutting a week’s groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the union cannot win paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning on repairs and continue looking for a paid opening rather than take an unpaid course. The union can still press for notice on cancelled days. I need a wage this month as much as a plan for 2034.

say: I would ask employers to explain **remaining jobs** before 2034 robots arrive.
I would keep demanding **cancelled-day notice** now.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots reach my repair work.
A cushion cannot grow from **three-day weeks** without a change in income.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** and continue the union roster log.
Enrol in **funded equipment training** only if it happens during paid shifts.
Apply for **school maintenance openings** after 2031 if any remain.
feel: **Anxious** about the current roster, with more time before robots.
S3.quote: I need a wage this month as much as a plan for 2034.
fieldNote: The longer warning does not erase **current short weeks** and less than one month of savings.
Yara’s training condition is **paid hands-on instruction** with safety checks, not generic willingness to retrain.

steps.text: Keep paid repair shifts and maintain the cancelled-day log
Ask the union to bargain for paid equipment training and shift notice
Enrol in funded hands-on equipment training if offered during paid shifts
Apply for paid school maintenance work after 2031 if openings remain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and capable site robots follow around 2039. A decade sounds long, but it does not pay next month's mortgage. I would ask local builders and the union what paid learning they will offer before they order machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots can do repairs. Our children will be grown, so school fees and pickup should no longer be the same burden. But I cannot assume a pension or a cleared mortgage, especially with wages this low and savings under a month now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working repairs and insist on a posted roster each week. My partner and I would first try to clear the grocery card in months with five paid days, then set aside a small amount only if there is money left. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the union for the contractor's robot schedule and apply for other paid building work if my shifts start to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about the next few years. A distant robot date gives me time to learn, but it does not fill the weeks we are missing today. I would feel better if the contractor fixed the roster before giving us a lecture on the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you set aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a full five-day week we might put a little aside after paying the grocery card, but there have not been many full weeks. I will not promise a number until the card balance stops growing. Even then, the mortgage comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children change where you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the children have left school, my partner and I could consider a longer commute for a paid job. That is still a family discussion, not an automatic move. We would need a real offer and a way to keep the mortgage paid during travel.

say: I would say **2039 robots** still leave next month’s mortgage unpaid.
I would ask for **paid learning** and a weekly roster now.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children but uncertain debt.
I cannot assume a **pension** or a cushion while current weeks remain short.
do: Keep paid **repair work** and demand posted weekly rosters.
Clear the **grocery card** in full-pay weeks before setting aside cash.
Ask the **union** for the robot schedule after 2036 and seek paid openings if shifts fall.
feel: Still **anxious** because current missing days matter more than the distant robot date.
S4.quote: A decade sounds long, but it does not pay next month's mortgage.
fieldNote: Yara keeps the **2039 robot date** separate from today’s much closer danger of cancelled paid days.
She treats grown children as a possible **commuting option**, not proof that retirement or mortgage relief will arrive.

steps.text: Keep paid flat-repair work and request a posted weekly roster
Pay down the grocery card in full-pay weeks before saving spare cash
Ask the union for the contractor robot schedule after 2036
Apply for other paid building openings if repair shifts disappear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots reach repair work around 2031, and my partner’s school cleaning may be exposed too. Written staffing plans, paid training during shifts and real local vacancies would help. Before that, a reliable weekly roster would help us pay this month’s mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a shift is cancelled the night before. A family cannot save for a robot date if it is already borrowing for groceries after a lost Friday. I want the employer to pay for proper notice and for safe learning time.

headlineQuote: A family cannot save for a robot date if it is already borrowing for groceries after a lost Friday.
portrait: Yara is an **experienced, certified** construction worker repairing occupied flats, with average trade skill and low pay.
Her partner’s **term-time cleaning** and less than a month saved leave two children and a mortgage exposed to cancelled days.
She has **never used AI** and seeks printed work plans, paid safety instruction and clear notice through the union.
Across scenarios she keeps **paid shifts** central, since few local builders offer an easy fallback.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable robots to both flat repairs and school cleaning around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **reliable roster**, written staffing plans, paid training and real local vacancies would help protect household income.
